title: Lone, Starless Cloud Could Be Hidden “Dark Galaxy,” Scientists Reveal】
body:
Astronomers have identified a compact cloud of hydrogen gas that appears to be completely devoid of stars, offering one of the most compelling pieces of evidence yet for the existence of an isolated “dark galaxy.” Detected with the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope (FAST) in Guizhou, China, the object contains roughly five hundred thousand solar masses of hydrogen yet shows no optical or infrared signature of any stellar population, suggesting it may be a massive, star‑free structure drifting alone in intergalactic space.

The discovery emerged from a targeted survey of high‑velocity clouds—large concentrations of neutral hydrogen moving at speeds that differ markedly from the rotation of the Milky Way. While many such clouds are known to be tidal debris or gas stripped from nearby galaxies, the newly found cloud, designated “FAST‑J0139+00,” stands out for its extreme compactness and isolation. Its radio emission, measured at the 21‑centimetre line of neutral hydrogen, reveals a velocity width of about 30 km s⁻¹ and a diameter of only a few hundred parsecs, dimensions that are comparable to dwarf galaxies but without any detectable starlight.

The notion of a dark galaxy—an object massive enough to be gravitationally bound yet lacking the luminous stars that normally betray a galaxy’s presence—has long intrigued astronomers. Theoretical models of galaxy formation predict that low‑mass dark matter halos should be abundant, but feedback processes such as supernova explosions and cosmic reionisation are thought to suppress star formation in many of them, leaving behind “failed” galaxies that are essentially invisible. Prior candidates have been identified through indirect methods, such as anomalous gas clouds or gravitational lensing signals, but none have combined the clear hydrogen signature with the absence of any optical counterpart as convincingly as this FAST detection.

The implications of confirming a dark galaxy are far‑reaching. First, it would provide a rare observational foothold for testing dark matter theories on small scales, where discrepancies between simulations and observations—often termed the “small‑scale crisis”—remain unresolved. If the cloud is indeed bound by a dark matter halo, its mass‑to‑light ratio would be orders of magnitude higher than that of typical dwarf galaxies, offering a natural laboratory for probing the nature of dark matter particles. Second, the existence of such an object would refine our understanding of the baryon budget in the local universe, helping to account for the “missing” ordinary matter that cosmological measurements predict but that has not yet been located in stars or hot gas.

Skepticism, however, remains warranted. Alternative explanations include the possibility that the cloud is a transient fragment of a larger, disrupted structure, or that it harbors a population of ultra‑faint stars below current detection thresholds. Follow‑up observations with deeper optical and infrared imaging, as well as higher‑resolution radio interferometry, will be crucial to rule out these scenarios. Moreover, measuring the cloud’s rotation curve could directly reveal the presence of a dark matter halo, a step that will likely require next‑generation facilities such as the Square Kilometre Array.

If subsequent studies confirm the dark galaxy hypothesis, the discovery could herald a new era in extragalactic astronomy, where the census of galaxies expands beyond the luminous to include a hidden population that has, until now, evaded detection. As FAST continues to scan the sky with unprecedented sensitivity, astronomers anticipate that more such enigmatic hydrogen clouds will surface, gradually illuminating the dark corners of the cosmic web and reshaping our picture of how galaxies, both bright and dark, assemble across the universe.
